title: Nicomachean Ethics
author: Aristotle
openingChapterLabel: Book I — The Good for Man
openingText: Every art, and every science reduced to a teachable form, and in like manner every action and moral choice, aims, it is thought, at some good: for which reason a common and by no means a bad description of the Chief Good is, "that which all things aim at." Now there plainly is a difference in the Ends proposed: for in some cases they are acts of working, and in others certain works or tangible results beyond and beside the acts of working: and where there are certain Ends beyond and beside the actions, the works are in their nature better than the acts of working.
about:
The Nicomachean Ethics is Aristotle's treatise on how to live well — what the human good is, how to identify virtues, how to develop them through habituation, what role pleasure and friendship play in a good life. The book is built around the concept of eudaimonia — usually translated as "happiness" or "flourishing" — and the claim that flourishing requires the lifelong cultivation of virtues, both intellectual and moral.

Aristotle taught it in Athens in the 4th century BCE. The text we have is probably his lecture notes, possibly compiled by his son Nicomachus (hence the name). It is the founding work of Western virtue ethics — a tradition that fell out of fashion in the early modern period and has been substantially revived in the last fifty years.

angleCards.title: Flourishing, not happiness.
angleCards.text: The word we translate as happiness — eudaimonia — does not mean a feeling. It means a life fully lived, in the exercise of distinctively human capacities. Aristotle's answer to "what should I want?" is more demanding and more interesting than modern self-help's version of the same question.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand eudaimonia as Aristotle meant it — not subjective happiness but the objective activity of living well — and see what that demands of a person across a lifetime.

angleCards.title: The mean between excess and deficiency.
angleCards.text: Courage sits between cowardice and recklessness. Generosity sits between miserliness and profligacy. For every virtue, Aristotle identifies two corresponding failures. The doctrine of the mean is not a call to mediocrity — it is a call to precision: hitting the right response, at the right time, toward the right person.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the doctrine of the mean through Aristotle's catalogue of virtues — and ask whether this framework actually tracks the moral reality of specific virtues or whether it strains under the weight of some of them.

angleCards.title: Friendship as the heart of a good life.
angleCards.text: Three books out of ten are on friendship. Aristotle believes no one would choose to live without friends, even with every other good. He distinguishes friendships of utility, pleasure, and virtue — and argues that the third kind, built on mutual admiration of character, is both rare and constitutive of who we become.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Nicomachean Ethics primarily through its treatment of friendship — what Aristotle thinks genuine friendship requires, why he gives it so much weight, and whether his three-tier distinction holds up.

angleCards.title: Practical wisdom as the master virtue.
angleCards.text: Phronesis — practical wisdom — is the capacity to see what a situation calls for and respond accordingly. It cannot be taught by rule. It is developed through experience, and it governs every other virtue. Aristotle argues that knowing ethics theoretically is nearly useless. The goal is to become a person who perceives and acts rightly.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the role of phronesis across the Ethics — how Aristotle distinguishes practical from theoretical knowledge, and what it means that good character cannot be reduced to following principles.

cast.name: Eudaimonia
cast.description: The end toward which all human action ultimately aims. Not a feeling of happiness but an activity — the ongoing exercise of one's distinctively human capacities in accordance with virtue. Aristotle argues you cannot have it for a moment; it takes a complete life.

cast.name: The Golden Mean
cast.description: Every virtue is the midpoint between two vices: excess on one side, deficiency on the other. Courage stands between recklessness and cowardice. The mean is not a fixed point — it varies by person, situation, and context. Hitting it requires practical wisdom, not a rule.

cast.name: Practical Wisdom (Phronesis)
cast.description: The intellectual virtue that governs all the others. It is the ability to perceive what a situation morally requires and to act accordingly — not by applying a principle but by seeing clearly. Aristotle thinks it cannot be taught directly; it must be grown through experience and habituation.

cast.name: Friendship (Philia)
cast.description: Aristotle devotes three of ten books to friendship, which tells you how seriously he takes it. He distinguishes three kinds — for utility, for pleasure, and for virtue — and argues that the highest form, in which each person values the other for their character, is both constitutive of the good life and extremely rare.

cast.name: Virtue (Arete)
cast.description: Not an act but a disposition — a stable tendency to feel, perceive, and respond in the right way. Virtues are acquired through habituation: you become courageous by doing courageous things. Once formed, they feel natural rather than effortful. The goal is not to control yourself but to become a person who wants the right things.

cast.name: Contemplation (Theoria)
cast.description: In Book X, Aristotle argues that the best human life is one devoted to philosophical contemplation — the activity most like divine existence, most self-sufficient, and most purely its own end. This apparently contradicts everything he said about virtuous civic life. The tension is real, and readers have argued about it ever since.

whyItMatters.title: A Theory of Happiness That Is Not About Feelings
whyItMatters.body: Aristotle's eudaimonia is not a state of mood but a quality of activity over a whole life. The argument is that you cannot know if someone has flourished until they are dead, and that flourishing requires cultivating dispositions over years. The argument is a rebuke to most modern theories of happiness.

whyItMatters.title: Virtue as Habit, Not Rule
whyItMatters.body: For Aristotle, becoming a good person is not about following rules but about developing habits — practicing courage until one is courageous, practicing generosity until one is generous. The model has shaped most serious thinking about character. It is also the philosophical root of the modern understanding that what we repeatedly do is what we become.

whyItMatters.title: The Mean Between Extremes
whyItMatters.body: Aristotle argues that most virtues are means between two excesses — courage between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between stinginess and waste. The doctrine of the mean is one of the most influential ideas in ethics. It has shaped how we describe virtues for two and a half millennia.
